mcqs.question: Why does a mistake in query understanding (e.g. a missed typo correction) compound so badly downstream in a search system?
options: Because typos are corrected automatically by the ranking model regardless of retrieval
Because query understanding errors only affect the ranking stage, not retrieval
Because retrieval then searches for entirely the wrong thing, and no amount of good ranking afterward can recover relevant results that were never retrieved in the first place
Because search engines discard any query containing a spelling error
mcqs.explanation: Query understanding runs before retrieval, so an error there means retrieval fetches candidates for the wrong query entirely — ranking can only reorder whatever retrieval returned, it can't add back documents that were never fetched. The other options misplace where in the pipeline the correction happens or invent behavior search systems don't actually have.

mcqs.question: Why is training or evaluating a ranker on raw click-through data risky without correcting for position bias?
options: Clicks are a perfectly unbiased measure of relevance and need no correction
Click data cannot be logged for more than the top 3 search results
Position bias only affects mobile search interfaces, not desktop
Users click higher-ranked results more often simply because they're seen first, so raw clicks reinforce whatever the current ranking already does rather than reflecting true relevance
mcqs.explanation: The core issue is a feedback loop: position, not just relevance, drives clicks, so uncorrected click data can make a mediocre-but-highly-placed result look better than a genuinely superior one ranked lower. Logging isn't limited to top-3, the bias isn't device-specific, and clicks are precisely not an unbiased relevance signal on their own.

mcqs.question: Why does BM25 discount a query term's weight by how common that term is across the whole document collection (inverse document frequency)?
options: So that rare, more informative terms (like a specific product name) contribute more to the score than common terms that appear in nearly every document and carry little discriminating power
So that documents with more words always score higher regardless of content
So that only the first occurrence of a term in a document is ever counted
So that queries with more than two words are rejected
mcqs.explanation: IDF weighting reflects that a term appearing in almost every document (like 'the') tells you little about relevance, while a rare term matching is a much stronger relevance signal — that's the entire point of discounting by document frequency. BM25 doesn't favor longer documents by default (it length-normalizes), doesn't cap counting to the first occurrence, and has no query-length restriction.

mcqs.question: Why can search systems cache query-understanding output and retrieval results more effectively than a typical feed-ranking system caches its results?
options: Because feeds never change their content, unlike search results
Because search catalogs are always smaller than social feed content pools

Because a meaningful share of search traffic is repeated head queries, so the same understanding/retrieval work can be reused across many requests for that same query text, unlike a feed where every user's session is unique
Because caching is impossible for feed ranking systems entirely
mcqs.explanation: The advantage comes from query repetition: many users issue the exact same head query text, so cached understanding and retrieval output serves many requests, whereas a feed's per-user personalized ranking has no equivalent repeated key to cache against as cleanly. Feed content does change, catalog size isn't the deciding factor, and feed systems do use caching, just for different things (like precomputed candidate pools).

mcqs.question: A search ranking model shows strong aggregate NDCG and click-through rate. What might still be hidden by these top-line numbers?
options: Nothing — strong aggregate metrics always mean every query segment is served well
The model could be performing poorly specifically on the long tail of rare queries, since high-volume head queries dominate the aggregate average and mask underperformance on infrequent ones
Aggregate metrics can only be computed for head queries, so tail performance is mathematically undefined
NDCG cannot be computed in aggregate across multiple queries at all
mcqs.explanation: Aggregate metrics are weighted by query volume, so a small number of high-frequency head queries can dominate the number while long-tail queries — each contributing negligibly to the average — quietly underperform without moving the aggregate at all. NDCG is well-defined across any query set including the tail, and strong aggregates don't guarantee uniform quality across segments.
